items.title: Sleep replays the day you want to keep
items.subtitle: Essay · 8 min
items.author: Plethora Lab notes
body: Memory does not finish when you close the book. During slow-wave sleep, the hippocampus replays traces laid down while you were awake.
That replay is not a luxury. Interrupt it and last night’s reading stays fragile. Protect it and the same pages become something you can use tomorrow.

passage.text: During slow-wave sleep, the hippocampus replays traces laid down while you were awake.

items.explain: Grounded in this essay: slow-wave sleep replays waking traces. The claim here is about consolidation timing, not a live model summary.

card.front: When does the hippocampus replay the day’s traces?

items.title: The Overnight Mind
items.subtitle: Chapter 2 · original field notes
items.author: M. Hale
body: We treated sleep as downtime because we could not watch it work. The overnight mind is not idle; it files.
Spacing what you reread across nights beats stacking another hour onto a tired afternoon.

passage.text: The overnight mind is not idle; it files.

items.explain: From this chapter: overnight rest is filing, not a blank. Spacing rereads across nights beats one long cram.

items.title: Spaced practice lab notes
items.subtitle: PDF · 3 pages
items.author: Learning methods desk
body: Page 1 — Protocol: 12 minutes of encoding, then a night of sleep, then a short retrieval probe.
Page 2 — Result: probes after sleep beat same-day probes on the same item set.
Page 3 — Caveat: the gain is for recall, not for rereading speed.

passage.text: Probes after sleep beat same-day probes on the same item set.

items.explain: The PDF’s result page states a sleep-spaced probe beat a same-day probe. This panel restates that sentence; it does not invent extra statistics.

card.front: In these lab notes, when did retrieval probes win?
card.back: After a night of sleep, not on the same day.

items.title: Encoding while you sleep
